2.3 Fighting and geographic spread of conflict

2.3.1 According to the RVI March 2026 report fighting between Tigrayan factions occurred on several occasions between July 2025 and February 2026. The first armed confrontation between the TPF and Tigray Security Force (TSF) took place on 1 July 2025 in Wejerat woreda, Southeastern Tigray, after a TPF unit crossed from Afar into the area. Further clashes occurred in Milazat on 29 July 2025, Dederba TibTam on 8 August 2025, and along the Tigray/Afar border between 2 and 7 November 2025. Fighting resumed between 29 January and 4 February 2026 in the Wajirat, Bala and Chercher border areas with TPF forces supported by ENDF drone strikes and artillery. TSF and ENDF forces also clashed in Tselemti between 26 and 31 January 2026, during which TSF regained control of large parts of Tselemti before subsequently withdrawing following an escalation in ENDF operations, including drone strikes inside Tigray.[footnote 32]

2.3.2 On 13 August 2026 ACLED reported clashes involving the TDF, the ENDF, Tekeze Zeb and Amhara security forces near the Ethiopia–Sudan border on 1 August 2026, with the ENDF reportedly securing control of the area. The ENDF and TDF subsequently reinforced their military positions. The TDF deployed additional forces in Southern Tigray and along the Tigray -Afar border while the ENDF conducted multiple drone strikes against TDF positions in Raya Alamata on 10 August. According to the ACLED report these developments reflected a significant escalation in hostilities and fears of renewed war between federal and Tigrayan forces had begun to materialise.[footnote 33]

2.3.3 The 27 August 2026, CTP Africa File reported that, following renewed fighting in Western Tigray on 1 August 2026, the ENDF conducted multiple drone strikes across Tigray, including in Mekelle and areas of Eastern, North-Western and Southern Tigray. Reportedly some strikes caused civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects. CTP also reported localised clashes between ENDF and TPLF forces during August 2026, including around Kobo in North Wollo Zone, Amhara region, Alamata in Southern Tigray, and May-Gaba in Western Tigray.[footnote 34]

2.3.4 On 1 September 2026, ACLED Senior Analyst Jalale Getachew Birru assessed that the renewed conflict in Tigray, which began in August 2026, was more localised and had not reached the scale or geographic spread of the 2020 to 2022 war. However, targeted armed clashes and aerial attacks continued to cause fatalities, with violence concentrated mainly in border areas and drone strikes reportedly focused on Mekelle.[footnote 35]

2.3.5 On 3 September 2026, the Economist, a UK-based subscription based international weekly news magazine covering global political, economic, and social issues[footnote 36] reported that Ethiopia carried out a series of airstrikes on Mekelle and other locations in Tigray during August 2026. The Economist also reported several clashes between the Ethiopian army and TPLF-affiliated forces.[footnote 37] On 12 September 2026, BBC Monitoring reported allegations from Tigrayan sources that Ethiopian government drone strikes had increased in southern Tigray. A reported drone strike on a primary school in Korem damaged school property, while 7 drone strikes in Hintalo District on 8 September 2026 reportedly killed 3 civilians and injured several others.[footnote 38]

2.3.6 On 24 September 2026, Deutsche Welle (DW), Germany’s state-funded international broadcaster[footnote 39] reported that TPLF forces had taken control of several airports in Tigray, including Mekelle Airport, amid continued clashes with government forces in Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire because of the security situation.[footnote 40] By 3 October 2026, ACLED reported that government and allied TPF forces had regained control of Mekelle and its airport after the TDF withdrew from the city following its encirclement the previous day.[footnote 41]

2.3.7 On 24 September 2026, AFP reported that the TPLF stated it was in a ‘full-blown war’ with the federal government. The TPLF reportedly seized 3 airports from federal police on 23 September and launched attacks into Afar and Amhara, taking control of Abala on the Tigray/Afar border, with further fighting reported around Yallo in Afar and Weldiya in Amhara.[footnote 42]

2.3.8 On 25 September 2026, ACLED reported that fighting had expanded across several fronts in northern Ethiopia, including along the Tigray-Amhara border, in Afar and western Tigray, with repeated drone strikes reported across Tigray and northern Amhara. Fighting involving federal forces, the Amhara Fano National Movement and TDF was reported in North Wello and Wag Hamera zones in Amhara and around the Tekeze River, Tslimoy and May Gaba in western Tigray. Drone strikes were also reported in southern and north-western Tigray. The fighting resulted in the suspension of flights at Lalibela Airport in Amhara on 24 September 2026.[footnote 43]

2.3.9 On 28 September 2026 Ethiopia Observer reported the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) evacuated 161 people from Mekelle to Semera in Afar. The evacuees included Ethiopian Federal Police personnel and their families, Ethiopian Airlines staff and their families, African Union monitors, and members of the Ethiopian Red Cross Society.[footnote 44]

2.3.10 On 30 September 2026 ACLED reported that suicide drones suspected to be linked with the Alliance for Survival targeted ENDF facilities in Bishoftu, Kombolcha and Bahir Dar. In response to the attacks and wider security concerns, the National Intelligence and Security Service (NISS) announced a prohibition on the use of drones in Addis Ababa.[footnote 45]

Reference: ETH-001-10-26

October 2026

Summary: Security situation in Tigray following the resumption of conflict

Summary

A breakdown in law and order or uncertain security situations do not in themselves give rise to a well-founded fear of persecution for a Refugee Convention reason.

In the absence of a link to one of the 5 Refugee Convention grounds necessary to be recognised as a refugee, the question to address is whether the person will face a real risk of serious harm in order to qualify for Humanitarian Protection (HP).

In the case of Elgafaji (C-465/07), the Grand Chamber of the European Court of Justice (ECJ) set out that

‘– the existence of a serious and individual threat to the life or person of an applicant for subsidiary protection is not subject to the condition that that applicant adduce evidence that he is specifically targeted by reason of factors particular to his personal circumstances;

‘– the existence of such a threat can exceptionally be considered to be established where the degree of indiscriminate violence characterising the armed conflict taking place … reaches such a high level that substantial grounds are shown for believing that a civilian, returned to the relevant country or, as the case may be, to the relevant region, would, solely on account of his presence on the territory of that country or region, face a real risk of being subject to that threat.’ (para 43).

Whilst a country guidance case on Iraq, in QD (Iraq) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2009] EWCA Civ 620 (24 June 2009) the Court of Appeal held that ‘We would accept UNHCR’s submission that, for the purposes of article 15(c), there is no requirement that the armed conflict itself must be exceptional. What is, however, required is an intensity of indiscriminate violence – which will self-evidently not characterise every such situation – great enough to meet the test spelt out by the ECJ [in Elgafaji, above].’ (para 36).

Tigray experienced a major armed conflict from 2020 to 2022, which formally ended with the Pretoria Agreement. However, continuing disputes over the Agreement’s implementation, divisions within the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), and tensions involving the federal government and TPLF contributed to renewed violence in early 2026, with fighting intensifying in August. In October 2026, the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) recaptured Mekelle from the TPLF and subsequently gained control of much of Tigray. A new caretaker regional administration was installed on 16 October 2026 (see Security development).

Although ENDF and TPF appeared to control most of Tigray, territorial control remained fluid and contested in some areas. Reporting in late October 2026 indicated that fighting continued in central Tigray, including around Rama and along the Abiy Addi axis, and in north-western Tigray, particularly north-west of Shire. Earlier reporting also placed TPLF forces in rural mountainous areas around Chila after withdrawing from Aksum (see Territorial control, Maps of territorial control and Fighting and geographic spread of conflict).

Between 1 January and 21 October 2026, the Armed Conflict Location and Events Data Project (ACLED) recorded 212 incidents of political violence and 253 combined civilian and combatant fatalities. A marked deterioration occurred in September, when incidents rose nearly fourfold from 15 in August to 59 events and fatalities surged from 17 to 115. During the same period ACLED’s civilian targeting filter identified 53 events and 19 fatalities. Civilian targeting captures events classified under other event types—such as explosions/remote violence and riots—where civilians were the main or only target (see Conflict dynamics, incidents and fatalities, Violence against civilians and ACLED ‘civilian targeting’ filter).

Even allowing for the spike in both total fatalities and civilian fatalities in September and October 2026, the levels of indiscriminate violence involving civilians are so low, relative to the size of the respective populations, that it cannot be said that the levels:

a. reach such a high level that substantial grounds are shown for believing that a civilian faces a real risk of serious harm simply by being present; and/or

b. are ‘great enough to meet the test spelt out by the ECJ’ [in Elgafaji].

Therefore, there are not substantial grounds for believing there is a real risk of serious harm in Tigray because of a serious and individual threat to a civilian’s life or person by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of international or internal armed conflict, as defined in paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

Even where there is not a real risk of serious harm by reason of indiscriminate violence in a situation of armed conflict in general, a person may still face a real risk of serious harm if they are able to show that there are specific reasons over and above simply being a civilian affected by indiscriminate violence.

However, paragraphs 339C and 339CA(iv) of the Immigration Rules only apply to civilians who must be non-combatants. This could include former combatants who have genuinely and permanently renounced armed activity.

Decision makers must consider each case on its facts.

te. Recognizing that key tasks were unfinished … the federal parliament on 1 April 2025 amended the law to extend the interim administration by up to one year. This was immediately applied to Tigray and the IRA’s mandate was extended to March 2026…

‘Along with the extension came a major reshuffle. On 8 April [2025], Abiy replaced Getachew with Tadesse as president of the IRA. The former TDF supremo who had been serving as an IRA vice-president, was seen as a relatively neutral, unifying figure above TPLF’s factional fray. In fact, his nomination to lead the IRA had been quietly supported by TPLF as a solution to remove Getachew without violence … Tadesse immediately assumed eight commitments upon taking office, including to facilitate IDP returns, complete disarmament, participate in the national dialogue, cease any unconstitutional foreign relations (presumed to refer to growing TPLF-Eritrea ties), lay groundwork for elections and uphold the rule of law.’[footnote 7]

1.1.5 The Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik - German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) is an independent German research institute that provides policy analysis on global political and security developments.[footnote 8] In a July 2026 article SWP stated that tensions between the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Ethiopian federal government stem primarily from unresolved issues arising from the implementation of the Pretoria Agreement. These include disputes over the status of territories occupied during the war, particularly areas claimed by both Tigray and the neighbouring Amhara region; the return of large numbers of internally displaced persons; the stalled demobilisation and reintegration of Tigray fighters; and the absence of agreed political arrangements to reintegrate Tigray into Ethiopia’s constitutional and electoral framework. The article also notes growing disagreements over the legitimacy and governance of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA), the legal status of the TPLF, and competing efforts by both Addis Ababa and Tigrayan political actors to shape the region’s future political order. As a result, the region remains in what the author describes as a “grey zone” between war and peace, characterised by political confrontation, sporadic armed clashes, and mutual accusations between the parties.[footnote 9]

1.1.6 International IDEA, an intergovernmental organisation that produces research and analysis on democracy, elections, governance, and constitutional processes, and provides technical support for democratic institutions worldwide[footnote 10] reported on its Global State of Democracy Initiative Ethiopia webpage:

‘On 8 April, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed extended the mandate of Lieutenant-General Tadesse Werede as head of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration by one year. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) rejected the move the next day as a unilateral breach of the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the two-year war in northern Ethiopia. On 19 April, the TPLF announced it would reinstate the region’s pre-war government, suspended under the deal, and accused the federal government of repeated violations. Tadesse, the region’s interim president, countered that reinstating the assembly would itself breach the deal, exposing a party rift. On 29 April, the TPLF urged Tadesse to cede power. The standoff has frozen the transition: the 1 June elections, meant to replace the interim administration with an elected Tigray government, are not expected to proceed there, freezing what Pretoria made temporary. The federal government has amassed forces along the region’s borders and restricted fuel and fiscal transfers, though international commentators noted these shortages, and the polls, may temper escalation.’[footnote 11]

1.1.7 Africa Confidential, an independent Africa-focused publication that provides political, security and economic reporting and analysis on developments across the continent[footnote 12] reported on 8 May 2026:

‘… [A]n emboldened Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) is stepping up its struggle with Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Angry at Addis Ababa’s unilateral one-year extension of the term of Tigray’s interim leader Lieutenant General Tadesse Werede, the TPLF’s Central Committee has restored the regional legislative council deemed unconstitutional by the federal government in the run-up to the Tigray-Addis Ababa war in 2020.

‘The TPLF now regards the 2022 Pretoria peace accord as defunct. On 5 May, the restored legislative council elected TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael as regional president, Kiros Hagos as speaker and Mihret Berhe as deputy speaker. Yet Addis Ababa has responded carefully, suggesting that despite the eroding Pretoria peace deal, it doesn’t favour immediate military escalation. The TPLF may have been confident of that when it made its provocative move …

‘The TPLF’s formal objection to extending Tadesse’s mandate was the absence of consultation stipulated by the Pretoria Agreement. Addis Ababa’s decision to sidestep talks with TPLF follows a pattern of denying the party legitimacy, following the banning of the party by the National Election Board of Ethiopia in May 2025 for non-compliance with regulatory requirements.

‘From TPLF’s perspective, approving Tadesse’s extension would confirm Addis Ababa’s authority over the region, stripping away any residual claim to Tigrayan self-administration, a pillar of the party’s identity.

‘Rejecting Tadesse’s extension, the TPLF described a pattern of violations, such as withholding budgetary transfers, fuel restrictions, and failure to return its territories. The party characterised it as a final rupture in the Pretoria deal.’[footnote 13]
